acc-u1-l1: A trader buys office furniture for ₦20,000 cash. Which entry is correct?
Furniture comes in (debit); cash goes out (credit). It is an asset, not goods for resale.
Is the furniture for resale or for use in the shop?
A business pays rent of ₦15,000 by cheque. Which entry is correct?
Rent expense is debited; a cheque reduces the bank balance, so Bank is credited.
A cheque comes from the bank, not the cash box.
Mama Ngozi buys goods for resale worth ₦10,000 on credit from Ade. Which entry is correct?
Goods come in (debit Purchases); Ade gave them on credit, so Ade becomes a creditor (credit).
Who is the giver if no cash is paid?
The owner brings ₦100,000 cash into the business to start it. Which entry is correct?
The business receives cash (debit); the owner gives capital (credit).
What does the business receive, and who gives it?
Which rule best describes double entry?
Debit the receiver, credit the giver
Debit the giver, credit the receiver
Each transaction has two sides: the account receiving value is debited and the one giving is credited.
Remember the Esusu book: what comes in goes on which side?
A shop makes cash sales of ₦7,000. Which entry is correct?
Cash comes in (debit Cash); goods go out as sales (credit Sales).
Cash comes in. What goes out?
A business pays wages of ₦5,000 in cash. Which entry is correct?
Wages is an expense (debit); cash leaves the business (credit).
The business pays its creditor, Ade, ₦10,000 by cheque. Which entry is correct?
Ade receives the payment (debit Ade); the bank pays (credit Bank).
A trader deposits ₦30,000 of shop cash into the bank. Which entry is correct?
Money moves from the cash box to the bank: Bank receives (debit), Cash gives (credit). This is a contra entry.
acc-u1-l2: A business sells goods on credit to Bola for ₦12,000. Which entry is correct?
Bola receives goods and owes (debit Bola); sales are made (credit Sales).
Bola returns goods worth ₦2,000 that were sold to him on credit. Which entry is correct?
Goods come back in (debit Returns Inwards); Bola owes less (credit Bola).
Bola gives the goods back. Who is the giver now?
Bola pays ₦10,000 cash towards what he owes. Which entry is correct?
Cash comes in (debit); Bola's debt reduces (credit Bola).
Bola gives cash. Credit the giver.
Someone who owes the business money
Someone the business owes money to
Debtors (trade receivables) owe the business, usually for goods bought on credit.
Think of Bola after a credit sale.
In which book are credit sales first recorded?
Credit sales are listed in the sales day book before being posted to the ledger.
Each kind of credit transaction has its own day book.
Returns inwards are goods coming back in from customers (sales returns).
'Inwards' means coming back in to us.
Bola bought ₦12,000 of goods on credit, returned ₦2,000 and then paid ₦6,000. What is the balance on his account?
Start with what he owed, then subtract returns and payments.
A business sells its old motor van (not stock) to Emeka on credit. Which entry is correct?
The van is an asset, not trading stock, so the Motor Van account is credited, not Sales.
Is the van something the business normally sells?
What kind of balance does a debtor's account normally have?
Debtors owe the business, so their accounts show debit balances (assets).
Debtors are assets. Which side are assets on?
acc-u1-l3: The owner takes ₦10,000 cash from the business for personal use. Which entry is correct?
Money taken for private use is drawings (debit); cash goes out (credit).
Is this a business expense or a private use?
The owner pays his child's school fees from the business bank account. Which entry is correct?
Debit School Fees Expense, Credit Bank
Private payments made with business money are drawings.
Are school fees a business cost?
At the end of the year, drawings are:
Treated as an expense in the profit and loss account
Drawings reduce the owner's capital; they are not business expenses.
Drawings take value OUT of what the owner has in the business.
Opening capital is ₦200,000, net profit is ₦50,000 and drawings are ₦30,000. What is the closing capital?
A shop owner takes goods costing ₦3,000 for family use. Which entry is correct?
Goods leave the business for private use: debit Drawings, credit Purchases at cost.
The goods were bought as purchases. Which account gives them up?
Which of these is NOT drawings?
The owner taking cash for personal use
Paying the owner's private electricity bill from the business account
Shop rent is a business expense; the others are private uses of business resources.
Which one benefits the business itself?
A trader uses business money to pay the rent on his own house. How is this treated?
The house is private, so the payment is drawings, not a business expense.
At the end of the year, the drawings account is closed by transferring its balance to:
Drawings reduce capital, so the balance is transferred to the capital account.
Opening capital ₦150,000; extra capital introduced ₦20,000; net loss ₦10,000; drawings ₦15,000. What is the closing capital?
A loss reduces capital, just like drawings.
acc-u1-l4: A debtor owes ₦20,000 and pays ₦19,000 in full settlement. What is the discount allowed?
Discount allowed = 20,000 - 19,000 = ₦1,000.
How much of the debt was forgiven?
How is discount allowed treated in the final accounts?
As an expense in the profit and loss account
As income in the profit and loss account
As a current asset
As capital
Discount allowed is a cost to the business, so it is an expense.
Does the business gain or lose by allowing a discount?
How is discount received treated in the final accounts?
As income in the profit and loss account
As an expense
As a liability
As drawings
Discount received is a gain, so it is added as income.
The business pays less than it owed. Is that a gain?
The business owes a supplier ₦8,000 and pays ₦7,600 in full settlement. What is the entry for the discount?
Debit Supplier, Credit Discount Received ₦400
Debit Discount Received, Credit Supplier ₦400
Debit Discount Allowed, Credit Supplier ₦400
Debit Supplier, Credit Bank ₦400
The supplier's account is cleared by ₦400 more (debit), and the discount is a gain (credit Discount Received).
The supplier forgave ₦400. Who gains?
How is a trade discount recorded in the books?
It is not recorded; goods are entered at the net price
Debit Discount Allowed
Credit Discount Received
In the cash book discount column
Trade discount is deducted before recording, so it never appears in the ledger.
Trade discount is taken off the list price at the time of sale.
A cash discount is given mainly to:
Encourage customers to pay promptly
Encourage customers to buy in bulk
Reduce the owner's capital
Pay staff wages
Cash discount rewards quick payment; trade discount rewards bulk or trade buyers.
When is the customer rewarded?
A customer who owes ₦40,000 pays promptly and is allowed a 5% cash discount. How much does he pay?
Discount = 5% of 40,000 = ₦2,000. Amount paid = ₦38,000.
Find 5%, then subtract it.
In a three-column cash book, the discount columns are:
Memorandum columns whose totals are posted to the discount accounts
Part of the bank balance
Never totalled
Only for VAT
Discount columns are not balanced; their totals are posted to the discount allowed and received accounts.
Is a discount a movement of cash?
The total of the discount allowed column in the cash book is ₦2,500. Where is it posted?
To the debit of the Discount Allowed account
To the credit of the Discount Allowed account
To the debit of the Bank account
To the credit of Sales
Discount allowed is an expense, so its total is debited to the Discount Allowed account.
Expenses go on which side?
acc-u1-l5: A trader sells goods for ₦33,000 including 10% VAT. How much VAT is included?
VAT is 10% of the NET price, not of the total.
Goods cost ₦50,000 before VAT. VAT is 7.5%. How much does the customer pay in total?
Add 7.5% of the price.
What is the standard rate of VAT in Nigeria since the Finance Act 2019?
The Finance Act 2019 raised VAT from 5% to 7.5%, effective February 2020.
It went up from 5%.
How is VAT collected on sales treated in the books?
As a liability owed to the tax authority (FIRS)
As income of the business
As an expense
As capital
The business collects VAT for the government, so it is owed to FIRS until paid.
Whose money is the VAT?
A sale of ₦11,000 includes 10% VAT. What is the net sales figure?
Divide by 1.10, not subtract 10% of the total.
Output VAT on sales is ₦9,000 and input VAT on purchases is ₦6,000. How much VAT must the business pay to FIRS?
VAT payable = output VAT - input VAT = 9,000 - 6,000 = ₦3,000.
The business can reclaim the VAT it paid on its purchases.
When goods are sold with VAT, the VAT part is credited to:
The VAT account
The Sales account
The Purchases account
The Capital account
Sales are credited with the net amount; the VAT portion is credited to the VAT account.
Should VAT inflate the sales figure?
A sale of ₦21,500 includes VAT at 7.5%. What is the net sales figure?
Divide by 1.075.
Input VAT is:
VAT paid by the business on its purchases
VAT charged by the business on its sales
A type of trade discount
A bank charge
Input VAT is paid on purchases and can be set against output VAT.
Input = coming in with purchases.
acc-u2-l1: A business has assets of ₦500,000 and liabilities of ₦200,000. What is its capital?
Capital is what is left after paying all debts.
Capital is ₦250,000 and liabilities are ₦50,000. What are the total assets?
Everything the business owns is financed by the owner (capital) or by others (liabilities).
Who provides the money for the assets?
A business buys stock worth ₦20,000 on credit. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
Stock (an asset) goes up; the creditor (a liability) goes up by the same amount.
What comes in, and who is now owed?
Assets are ₦400,000 and capital is ₦320,000. What are the liabilities?
Which of these is a liability?
A bank overdraft is money owed to the bank, so it is a liability.
Which one does the business owe?
Which of these is a current asset?
Stock is expected to be sold within a year, so it is a current asset.
Which one turns into cash quickly?
A business pays a creditor ₦10,000 in cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
Cash (asset) goes down and the creditor (liability) goes down by the same amount.
Cash leaves, and a debt is cleared.
A shop has cash ₦20,000, stock ₦60,000, equipment ₦120,000 and creditors ₦40,000. What is the owner's capital?
acc-u2-l2: Sales ₦150,000; opening stock ₦20,000; purchases ₦90,000; closing stock ₦30,000. What is the gross profit?
Work out cost of goods sold first.
Cost of goods sold is calculated as:
You start with opening stock, add what you bought, and remove what is left at the end.
Think of what was available, then what is left.
Sales are ₦80,000 and cost of goods sold is ₦50,000. What is the gross profit?
Gross profit = sales - cost of sales.
Opening stock ₦10,000; purchases ₦60,000; closing stock ₦15,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
Add opening stock, subtract closing stock.
Gross profit is ₦40,000 on sales of ₦160,000. What is the gross profit margin?
How are returns inwards treated in the trading account?
Returns inwards are goods customers sent back, so they reduce sales.
Goods came back from customers. Did you really sell them?
Added to the cost of purchases in the trading account
Carriage inwards is the cost of bringing goods in, so it is part of the cost of goods.
It is a cost of getting the goods to your shop.
Sales ₦200,000; returns inwards ₦10,000; cost of goods sold ₦120,000. What is the gross profit?
Goods costing ₦80,000 are sold at a mark-up of 25% on cost. What is the gross profit?
acc-u2-l3: Gross profit ₦90,000; rent ₦15,000; salaries ₦30,000; commission received ₦5,000. What is the net profit?
Net profit is what remains after all expenses and other income are taken into account.
Gross profit is ₦60,000 and total expenses are ₦70,000. What is the result?
Expenses exceed gross profit by ₦10,000, giving a net loss.
Are expenses bigger than gross profit?
Which of these is an expense in the profit and loss account?
Electricity is a running cost of the business; the others are assets, capital or drawings.
Which one is a regular running cost?
How is discount received treated in the profit and loss account?
Added to gross profit as income
Discount received is a gain, so it is added as other income.
Is it a gain or a cost?
GP ₦120,000; wages ₦40,000; depreciation ₦10,000; bad debts ₦5,000; discount allowed ₦3,000. What is the net profit?
Add all the expenses, then subtract.
A business buys a new delivery van for ₦2,000,000. Where does this appear?
In the balance sheet as a non-current (fixed) asset
As an expense in the profit and loss account
Buying a van is capital expenditure, so it is shown as an asset; only its depreciation is an expense.
Will the van be used for many years?
GP ₦50,000; rent received ₦8,000; total expenses ₦33,000. What is the net profit?
Net profit for the year is added to:
Profit belongs to the owner, so it increases capital in the balance sheet.
acc-u2-l4: Debtors total ₦60,000 and a 5% provision for doubtful debts is created. What net debtors figure appears in the balance sheet?
Find the provision, then subtract it.
When a provision for doubtful debts of ₦4,000 is first created, the ₦4,000 is:
Debited to the profit and loss account as an expense
Credited to the profit and loss account as income
Added to debtors
Added to capital
Creating the provision is a charge (expense) against profit.
Is the business expecting to gain or lose?
Debtors are ₦100,000 and the provision for doubtful debts is 2%. What is the provision?
Find 2% of the debtors.
The provision for doubtful debts increases from ₦3,000 to ₦5,000. What is charged to the profit and loss account?
Only the increase, ₦2,000, is charged this year.
Only the CHANGE affects this year's profit.
The provision for doubtful debts falls from ₦6,000 to ₦4,000. How is this treated in the profit and loss account?
₦2,000 is added as a gain
₦2,000 is charged as an expense
₦4,000 is charged as an expense
₦10,000 is added as a gain
A decrease in the provision is written back to profit as a gain.
A smaller provision means less expected loss.
Debtors are ₦50,000. A bad debt of ₦2,000 is written off, then a 10% provision is made. What is the provision?
Debtors after write-off = 48,000. Provision = 10% * 48,000 = ₦4,800.
Write off the bad debt BEFORE working out the provision.
A debt of ₦1,500 is written off as bad. Which entry is correct?
Debit Bad Debts, Credit the Debtor
Debit the Debtor, Credit Bad Debts
Debit Cash, Credit Bad Debts
Debit Bad Debts, Credit Sales
The loss is an expense (debit Bad Debts) and the debtor no longer owes (credit Debtor).
The debtor won't pay. Remove the debt.
Why do businesses create a provision for doubtful debts?
To be prudent and allow for debts that may not be paid
To increase profit
To pay creditors
To increase the value of debtors
The prudence concept requires the business to allow for likely losses.
Which accounting concept says don't overstate assets?
How is the provision for doubtful debts shown in the balance sheet?
Deducted from debtors under current assets
Added to debtors
Shown as a liability
Added to capital
Debtors are shown less the provision, to give the amount expected to be collected.
What value of debtors do you really expect to collect?
acc-u2-l5: Sales ₦300,000; opening stock ₦20,000; purchases ₦180,000; closing stock ₦40,000; expenses ₦60,000. What is the net profit?
Gross profit first, then subtract expenses.
Sales ₦400,000; cost of goods sold ₦250,000; expenses ₦100,000; other income ₦10,000. What is the net profit?
Don't forget the other income.
Sales ₦250,000; opening stock ₦30,000; purchases ₦150,000; closing stock ₦20,000; rent ₦25,000; wages ₦35,000. What is the net profit?
Step by step: COGS, GP, then NP.
Sales ₦120,000; returns inwards ₦5,000; cost of goods sold ₦70,000; expenses ₦30,000. What is the net profit?
Deduct returns inwards from sales first.
Sales are ₦180,000 with a gross profit margin of 40%. Expenses are ₦50,000. What is the net profit?
Margin is a percentage of sales.
Net sales ₦500,000; gross profit ₦200,000; net profit ₦80,000; there is no other income. What are the total expenses?
Expenses are the gap between gross and net profit.
Sales ₦90,000; opening stock ₦10,000; purchases ₦60,000; closing stock ₦15,000; expenses ₦20,000. What is the net profit?
Opening + purchases - closing.
Opening capital ₦300,000; net profit ₦50,000; drawings ₦20,000. What is the closing capital?
Profit adds to capital; drawings reduce it.
Sales ₦600,000; cost of goods sold ₦420,000; expenses ₦150,000; discount received ₦6,000. What is the net profit?
Discount received is income.
acc-u3-l1: A delivery van costs ₦250,000, has a scrap value of ₦50,000 and a useful life of 4 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
Subtract the scrap value first.
Equipment costs ₦80,000 with no scrap value and a useful life of 5 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
Cost divided by life.
The straight-line depreciation formula is:
(Cost - scrap value)/useful life
Cost * useful life
(Cost + scrap value)/useful life
Scrap value/useful life
Spread the cost less what you'll get back at the end evenly over the asset's life.
What part of the cost is actually used up?
A machine costs ₦60,000, has a scrap value of ₦6,000 and a 6-year life. What is the annual depreciation?
Cost minus scrap, then divide by 6.
Under the straight-line method, depreciation is:
The same amount every year
Higher in the early years
Higher in the later years
Only charged in the first year
Straight-line spreads the cost equally, so each year gets the same charge.
Picture a straight line on a graph.
Equipment costs ₦120,000, scrap value ₦20,000, life 10 years. What is its net book value after 3 years?
NBV = cost - accumulated depreciation.
Depreciation is best described as:
Spreading the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
Money saved to buy a new asset
An increase in the value of an asset
Cash paid to the owner
Depreciation allocates the cost of an asset to the years that benefit from it.
Does depreciation involve paying out cash?
A tricycle costs ₦400,000 and is depreciated at 20% per annum on cost (straight-line). What is the annual depreciation?
Straight-line on cost: the same 20% of cost each year.
Which of these is NOT a cause of depreciation?
An increase in the asset's market value
Wear and tear
Obsolescence
Passage of time
Depreciation comes from wear, obsolescence and time; a rise in market value is not a cause.
Which one makes the asset worth more?
acc-u3-l2: A machine costing ₦240,000 is bought on 1 April. The year ends on 31 December. Depreciation is 10% per annum, straight-line, by months owned. What is the first year's charge?
Count the months from April to December.
Equipment costing ₦100,000 is bought on 1 October. The year ends 31 December. Depreciation is 20% straight-line, by months owned. What is the first year's charge?
October, November, December.
A full year's depreciation on an asset is ₦24,000. It was bought exactly halfway through the year. With time apportionment, what is the first year's charge?
Half a year means half the charge.
An asset costing ₦80,000 is bought on 1 July. The year ends 30 June the following year. Depreciation is 15% straight-line. What is the first year's charge?
From 1 July to 30 June is a full 12 months: 15% * 80,000 = ₦12,000.
How many months from 1 July to the next 30 June?
A machine costing ₦60,000 is bought on 1 March. The year ends 31 December. Depreciation is 10% straight-line, by months owned. What is the first year's charge?
Count from March to December.
A business charges a full year's depreciation in the year of purchase. It buys a ₦50,000 computer in November and depreciates at 20%. What is the charge for that year?
The policy charges a full year regardless of the month: 20% * 50,000 = ₦10,000.
Read the business's policy carefully.
A ₦360,000 generator is bought on 1 May. The year ends 31 December. Depreciation is 25% straight-line, by months owned. What is the first year's charge?
May to December is 8 months.
Charging depreciation 'on a month-by-month basis' means:
Charging only for the months the asset was owned in the year
Charging a full year regardless
Charging nothing in the first year
Charging twice in the first year
Time apportionment matches the charge to the months the asset was used.
Match the charge to the time the asset was owned.
The ₦240,000 machine bought on 1 April (10% straight-line) is kept for the whole of the second year. What is the second year's charge?
In a full year the charge is 10% * 240,000 = ₦24,000.
In the second year it is owned all 12 months.
acc-u3-l3: A truck costs ₦400,000 and is depreciated at 25% per annum, reducing balance. What is the depreciation in year 1?
In year 1, the reducing balance is the cost.
For the same ₦400,000 truck at 25% reducing balance, what is the depreciation in year 2?
Apply the rate to the NEW balance.
A machine costing ₦200,000 is depreciated at 10% reducing balance. What is the depreciation in year 2?
Find the balance at the start of year 2.
The reducing balance method charges:
More depreciation in the early years and less later
The same amount each year
Less in the early years and more later
No depreciation in year 1
Because the rate applies to a falling balance, the charge falls each year.
What happens to the balance each year?
A bus costs ₦1,000,000 and is depreciated at 20% reducing balance. What is the depreciation in year 3?
Work year by year.
Under the reducing balance method, each year's depreciation equals:
The rate * the net book value at the start of the year
The rate * the original cost
Cost divided by useful life
The scrap value * the rate
The rate is applied to the remaining (reducing) balance each year.
Which value does the percentage apply to?
Equipment costs ₦50,000 and is depreciated at 40% reducing balance. What is the depreciation in year 1?
Year 1 uses the cost.
For which kind of asset is the reducing balance method most suitable?
Assets like vehicles that lose most of their value early
Land, which does not wear out
Assets that gain value
Assets used equally every year with no early loss
Vehicles lose value fast at first, which reducing balance reflects.
Which asset loses value fastest when new?
A machine costs ₦600,000 and is depreciated at 30% reducing balance. What is the depreciation in year 2?
Find the NBV after year 1 first.
acc-u3-l4: A machine costing ₦100,000 is depreciated at 20% reducing balance. What is its net book value after 2 years?
An asset costing ₦400,000 is depreciated at 50% reducing balance. What is its net book value after 2 years?
A computer costing ₦80,000 is depreciated at 25% reducing balance. What is its net book value after 2 years?
Net book value is calculated as:
NBV is what remains of the cost after taking off all depreciation so far.
What is left of the cost?
A van costing ₦500,000 is depreciated at 10% reducing balance. What is its net book value after 2 years?
An asset costs ₦300,000 and its accumulated depreciation is ₦120,000. What is its net book value?
A machine costing ₦200,000 (no scrap) is depreciated at 20% straight-line. What is its net book value after 3 years?
A generator costs ₦1,000,000 and is depreciated at 20% reducing balance. What is its net book value after 3 years?
Under the reducing balance method, does the net book value ever reach zero?
No, it keeps falling but never quite reaches zero
A percentage of a positive balance always leaves something, so NBV never reaches zero.
What is 80% of a small number?
acc-u3-l5: A machine cost ₦90,000; accumulated depreciation is ₦40,000. It is sold for ₦45,000. What is the result?
NBV = 50,000. Sold for 45,000, which is ₦5,000 less than NBV: a loss.
Compare the sale price with the NBV.
Equipment cost ₦120,000; accumulated depreciation is ₦70,000. It is sold for ₦60,000. What is the result?
How is a profit on disposal of an asset treated?
As income (credit) in the profit and loss account
As an expense in the profit and loss account
A gain on disposal increases profit, so it is credited to the P&L.
A fully depreciated old computer (cost ₦50,000, accumulated depreciation ₦50,000) is sold for ₦3,000. What is the result?
NBV is zero, so the whole ₦3,000 is a profit.
What is the NBV of a fully depreciated asset?
When an asset is sold, its original cost is transferred by:
Debit Disposal account, Credit Asset account
Debit Asset account, Credit Disposal account
The asset is removed at cost: the asset account is credited and the disposal account debited.
Remove the asset from its account.
When an asset is sold, its accumulated depreciation is transferred by:
Debit Provision for Depreciation, Credit Disposal account
Debit Disposal account, Credit Provision for Depreciation
The accumulated depreciation is cleared out and credited to the disposal account.
The provision account has a credit balance. How do you close it?
An asset is sold for cash. How is the sale price recorded?
Cash comes in (debit); the proceeds go to the disposal account (credit), not to Sales.
It's not trading stock, so it doesn't go to Sales.
An asset with a cost of ₦200,000 and an NBV of ₦80,000 is sold for ₦70,000. What is the result?
Sale price 70,000 is ₦10,000 less than NBV 80,000: a loss.
Compare the price with the NBV, not the cost.
A generator cost ₦150,000 and was depreciated at 20% per annum, straight-line, for 2 years. It is then sold for ₦100,000. What is the result?
